paras: The lynching of Rube Carothers took place on the night of August 16, 1880, near Greenvine, Texas, when masked men took Carothers, a Black man accused of selling stolen cattle, from the guards holding him during his preliminary examination and hanged him from a cottonwood tree. A coroner's jury found that he had been hanged by persons unknown. Wire reports carried the killing nationally, while the Brenham Weekly Banner printed a local letter and the presiding justice's statement.

According to a letter from Burton signed "H. R. V. B.", farmers around Greenvine had missed cattle about three weeks earlier, and eleven head were traced to a butcher at New Ulm who had bought them from Carothers and Andrew Jackson. Justice C. G. Campbell gave a different count, fifteen head valued at $220, which he said Carothers had sold with the help of "two other colored men".
Carothers was arrested and brought before Campbell on August 12 and held in the Brenham jail while the hearing was postponed for counsel and witnesses; Jackson remained at large.

On August 16 Carothers was brought from Brenham to Greenvine for the examination, which ran until dark with witnesses still to be heard. Both local accounts say he cursed the court and the witnesses; Campbell attributed this to drink and was told that Deputy Sheriff Jack Lands had given him a half-pint of whiskey on the way. Campbell adjourned until eight the next morning and deputized William Brandt to keep the prisoner, and Brandt summoned three men to help him.

The Burton letter says the guard, "fearing violence", moved Carothers to a rent house after the crowd dispersed. By the guards' report, at about a quarter to eleven that night some fifty masked men charged them and took the prisoner by force. He was carried about three-quarters of a mile, and his body was found around nine the next morning hanging from a cottonwood tree in Labahia prairie.

An inquest examined five witnesses, and the jury found that Carothers died by hanging "by the neck with a new grass rope" at the hands of persons unknown to them. No report of arrests or prosecution of the masked men appears in the coverage.

In a statement dated August 21, Campbell answered "some of the friends of deceased" who, he wrote, were questioning his conduct, saying he had not known of any organized mob waiting when he adjourned. Lands then came to the Banner office to deny supplying the whiskey, saying he had given Carothers $1.25 of his own money, and the paper declined to print the rest of his document unless he paid for it.

The Brenham Weekly Banner ran the Burton letter under the headline "JUDGELYNCH. A Cottonwood Tree Bears Strange Fruit", with a subhead saying Carothers "adorns a Limb". Its writer called the killing "deplorable" but "the natural outgrowth" of low morals among "a large portion of our population" and of an uncertain criminal law, adding that Carothers had boasted and threatened his accusers. Campbell's own statement declined to judge the act, leaving "justifiacation or condemnation" to the people.

Outside Texas the killing ran as a short Brenham dispatch of August 19, credited by the Richmond Dispatch to the Galveston News, calling Carothers "colored" and on trial for stealing cattle. Papers in Washington, Salt Lake City, Cheyenne and Chillicothe printed it, often misspelling the town "Benham", "Berham" or "Bernham". Weekly news summaries repeated it a week later as the lynching of "a colored cattle thief".

Most of these items carried no comment, but the Wheeling Register headed the dispatch "TEXAS STYLE. Now if He Had Only Killed Two or Three Men-", a sardonic remark on lynching a man for cattle theft. The Chicago Tribune called him "a horse-thief" and the Sacramento Daily Record-Union "an alleged cattle thief".

The wire said Carothers was taken from the jail at Brenham by forty men, but the two local accounts, one from the presiding justice, place the seizure near Greenvine and are the closer sources. Wire copies also dated it Tuesday night, Tuesday morning, Wednesday night or the night of the 18th, against the 16th in Campbell's account.

reader.title: Lynching of Rube Carothers
bases: A band of 40 to 50 masked men took a Black prisoner awaiting the end of his preliminary examination from his guards and hanged him from a tree (A1, A11, A2).

Carothers was hanged by masked men who overpowered his guards, and the coroner's jury found he died by hanging at the hands of persons unknown (A11, A1); the wire put the band at forty and Justice Campbell's statement at about fifty, and the seizure followed a hearing on a cattle-theft charge (A2, A11).

The local Burton letter, Justice Campbell's statement with the coroner's verdict, and a separate Galveston News dispatch from Brenham all report the seizure and hanging (A1, A11, A4), though they differ on place, date and numbers.

accounts.label: Local correspondent (Burton letter)
accounts.gist: After a Monday hearing at Greenvine in which Carothers cursed the court, a special constable fearing violence moved him to a rent house, where a disguised mob took him in the night and hanged him from a cottonwood about three-quarters of a mile away.

accounts.label: Justice C. G. Campbell and coroner's jury
accounts.gist: The hearing of the 16th was adjourned at dark; about 10:45 p.m. some 50 masked men charged the deputy and his three guards and took the prisoner, whose body was found next morning in Labahia prairie; the jury found death by hanging at the hands of persons unknown.

accounts.label: Wire report (Galveston News special from Brenham)
accounts.gist: Carothers, on trial for stealing cattle, was taken out of jail at Brenham on Tuesday night by forty masked men who overpowered the guards.

accounts.label: Second wire version
accounts.gist: While under guard 'last night' (in a dispatch dated the 19th), the guards were overpowered by forty disguised men and Carothers lynched.

framing.detail: The Brenham Banner headlined the letter 'JUDGELYNCH. A Cottonwood Tree Bears Strange Fruit', and the writer called the act deplorable yet 'the natural outgrowth' of low morals and an uncertain criminal law, adding the victim's alleged boasts and threats.
Justice Campbell's statement in the Banner defended his own conduct and left 'justifiacation or condemnation' of the lynching to the people.
The Wheeling Register ran the wire under 'TEXAS STYLE. Now if He Had Only Killed Two or Three Men-', a sardonic line on the lynching of a man charged only with cattle theft.
Most papers outside Texas ran one-line wire or news-summary items calling him 'colored' and a 'cattle thief' or 'alleged cattle thief'.

record_check.dossier: Night of 1880-08-16 per the two local accounts (hearing on the 16th, seized about 10:45 p.m., body found next morning); wires give the 17th or 18th
Greenvine (rent house near the justice's court; hanged in Labahia prairie); Brenham appears only in the wire dateline and the 'out of jail' version
Not settled by the texts; the Burton letter's phrase 'justice Campbell, of Greenvine, in Austin county' is the only county named for the hearing
One victim, Rube (Reuben) Carothers; 'Reuben Carolhcrs' is an OCR variant of the same name, not a second victim
Accused of selling stolen cattle (theft of stock); he claimed to have bought them
Name is Rube Carothers; the guard was William Brandt, deputized by Justice Campbell, with three helpers; an inquest found death at the hands of persons unknown
